families.title: Tile gardens: squares
families.mathematics: Square pieces on a rectangle. The biggest-square rule cuts the largest square from one end and repeats on what is left. Cutting a × b to (a − b) × b keeps every common divisor and the sides shrink, so the last square has side gcd(a, b), the largest square whose equal copies fill the rectangle: Euclid’s algorithm, drawn. The counts of equal squares are the partial quotients of the continued fraction of the sides, and the most sizes within a range come from consecutive Fibonacci numbers (13 by 8 has five within 15). The rule is not always fewest: 6 by 5 needs 5 squares where the rule uses 6, and 13 by 11 needs 6 where it uses 8. With only 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares, a rectangle fills exactly when both sides are even, both are multiples of 3, or one side is a multiple of 6. A row of odd length can’t be all 2s, so a 3 by 3 square crosses it; more such lines, three apart, than 3 by 3 squares fit is a certificate that it can’t be filled.
rules: Squares of any whole size, with edges on the grid lines, no gaps and no overlaps.
Done says no filling uses fewer squares. The app checks; if fewer fit, it says so, and that count stays answered.

puzzles.title: Squares playground
puzzles.objective: Size a rectangle and cut its biggest squares one at a time.
puzzles.instruction: Size a rectangle and cut its biggest squares one at a time.
puzzles.controls: Tap a square of the grid to stretch the rectangle to it, or drag its corner; arrow keys move the corner too. Cut takes the biggest square off one end of what is left; press it again for the next.
rules: The biggest-square rule cuts the largest square from one end of the rectangle and repeats on what is left. The last square it cuts is ringed.
puzzles.idea: Free play with the biggest-square rule. The cuts are forced, so this is for watching them, not a puzzle.
puzzles.prerequisites: None: the app cuts the squares. Reading numbers to 15 helps.
hints: Make a long thin rectangle and cut it.
Make a rectangle whose sides are both even. What is its last square?
Try 13 by 8.

parent.notice: Whether your child starts to say the next square before pressing Cut.
parent.prompt: Which rectangles end with a big last square?
parent.explanation: Cutting the biggest square from an a by b rectangle leaves (a − b) by b, which has the same common divisors, so the last square has side gcd(a, b): Euclid’s algorithm, drawn.
parent.extension: Find a rectangle that takes many cuts but is not very big.

puzzles.provenance: Week 32, the shared rule and its 5 by 2 example on every packet’s first page; the card calls tapping through the forced cuts a playground.

puzzles.title: Four threes
puzzles.objective: Make two rectangles from the four 3 by 3 squares whose last squares are different sizes.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make two rectangles with different last squares.
puzzles.instruction: Make two rectangles from the four 3 by 3 squares whose last squares are different sizes.
puzzles.controls: Tap where a square’s top-left corner goes, or drag one out from a corner. Tap a square to lift it; Clear lifts them all.
rules: Each rectangle uses all four 3 by 3 squares, side to side.

When the four make a rectangle, the app runs the rule on it. The biggest-square rule cuts the largest square from one end of the rectangle and repeats on what is left. The last square it cuts is ringed.
A rectangle turned round is the same one.
puzzles.idea: Four equal squares make a long strip or a big square, and the rule ends on a different size for each: 3 for 12 by 3, 6 for 6 by 6.
puzzles.prerequisites: None: tap to place squares. The app runs the rule.
hints: Put the four squares side to side to make a rectangle, and look at its last square.
Lift them and make a different rectangle.
One row of four, then two rows of two. The rule cuts 6 by 6 in one piece.

parent.notice: Whether your child makes both the strip and the big square, and sees that the big square is cut in one piece.
parent.prompt: Why does the long one end on a 3 and the big square on a 6?
parent.explanation: Four 3 by 3 squares fill only two rectangles, 12 by 3 and 6 by 6, up to turning. The rule cuts 12 by 3 into four 3s, so its last square is 3, and cuts 6 by 6 in one piece, a 6. The last square is always the largest square whose equal copies fill the rectangle: 3 fills 12 by 3 and 6 does not; 6 fills 6 by 6.
parent.extension: Which rectangles can six 2 by 2 squares make? Do their last squares match? (12 by 2 and 6 by 4 both end on 2.)
parent.connection: The last square of the biggest-square rule is the greatest common divisor of the sides.

puzzles.provenance: Week 32 K–1 Problem 5: every rectangle of four 3 by 3 squares (3 by 12 and 6 by 6) and whether their last squares match.

puzzles.title: Four by three
puzzles.objective: Fill the rectangle with as few squares as you can, then press Done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with as few squares as you can.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the rectangle with as few squares as you can, then press Done.
puzzles.controls: Drag from one corner of a square to the opposite corner, or tap the two corners; tap one square twice for the smallest square. Tap a square to lift it; Clear lifts them all. Press Done when you think no filling uses fewer squares.
rules: Squares of any whole size, with edges on the grid lines, no gaps and no overlaps.
Done says no filling uses fewer squares. The app checks; if fewer fit, it says so, and that count stays answered.
puzzles.idea: Biggest first works here: a 3 by 3 and three 1s. Three squares can’t fill it.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start: drag squares from corner to corner. Counting to about ten; square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25) help explain why fewer can’t fit.
hints: Fill it, then count. Could fewer squares fill it?
Try the biggest square that fits first.
A 3 by 3 and three 1 by 1 squares make four. Could three squares have area 12?

parent.notice: Whether your child counts the squares and tries for fewer before pressing Done.
parent.explanation: A 3 by 3 and three 1s make four. Fewer can’t: one or two of the square numbers 1, 4 and 9 never add to 12, and the only three that do are 4 + 4 + 4. Three 2 by 2 squares in a rectangle 3 tall would each take two of its rows, so no two can sit one above the other; side by side they need 6 across, and there are 4.
parent.extension: Is the biggest square first always fewest? Puzzle 4 says no.
parent.connection: How few squares can tile a rectangle is a research question (Kenyon, 1996).

puzzles.provenance: Week 32 bonus Problem 1, the 4 by 3 board, where the rule’s four is fewest.

puzzles.title: Five by two
puzzles.objective: Fill the rectangle with 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares, or press Can’t and pick rows or columns that each need their own 3 by 3 square, more than fit.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the rectangle with 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares, or press Can’t and pick rows or columns that each need their own 3 by 3 square, more than fit.
puzzles.controls: Drag from one corner of a square to the opposite corner, or tap the two corners; tap one square twice for the smallest square. Tap a square to lift it; Clear lifts them all. Only 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares. Once a square is down, Can’t puts a tab beside each row and below each column: tap tabs to pick lines, and tap a tab again to drop it.
rules: Only 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares, with edges on the grid lines, no gaps and no overlaps.
Solved when the rectangle is full, or with a right Can’t.

Can’t comes after a try, with at least one square on the board. Then pick rows, or columns, that each need a 3 by 3 square of their own, more of them than 3 by 3 squares fit. One 3 by 3 square crosses three neighbouring lines, so picked lines are at least three apart; a row and a column can share one.
puzzles.idea: A row of 5 can’t be all 2s, so it needs a 3 by 3 square, and none fits in 2 rows.
puzzles.prerequisites: Telling odd lengths from even; counting to 7. Reading the Can’t rule with a grown-up the first time.
hints: Try to fill it. What is left over?
Can 2 by 2 squares make a row of 5?
Press Can’t and tap one row.

parent.notice: Whether your child sees that 2s only make even lengths.
parent.prompt: Why does a row of 5 need a 3?
parent.explanation: Every square that crosses a row covers 2 or 3 of its squares. 2s alone always cover an even number, so a row of 5 needs a 3 by 3 square across it. A 3 by 3 square is taller than this rectangle, so it can’t be filled.
parent.extension: Which strips 2 tall can be filled? (Even lengths, with 2s.)
parent.connection: Even plus even is even: a parity argument.

puzzles.provenance: New: an entry to Week 32 bonus Problem 3 (fill with only 2s and 3s).

puzzles.title: Six by five
puzzles.objective: Fill the rectangle with as few squares as you can, then press Done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with as few squares as you can.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the rectangle with as few squares as you can, then press Done.
puzzles.controls: Drag from one corner of a square to the opposite corner, or tap the two corners; tap one square twice for the smallest square. Tap a square to lift it; Clear lifts them all. Press Done when you think no filling uses fewer squares.
rules: Squares of any whole size, with edges on the grid lines, no gaps and no overlaps.
Done says no filling uses fewer squares. The app checks; if fewer fit, it says so, and that count stays answered.
puzzles.idea: The rule cuts a 5 by 5 and five 1s, six squares; five fit, two 3s over three 2s.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start: drag squares from corner to corner. Counting to about ten; square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25) help explain why fewer can’t fit.
hints: Fill it the biggest-square way and count.
Try squares that are not the biggest: a 6 by 3 strip and a 6 by 2 strip.
Two 3 by 3 squares fill one strip and three 2 by 2 squares the other.

parent.notice: Many children put the 5 by 5 down first and end with six.
parent.prompt: Is the biggest square first always fewest?
parent.explanation: The rule uses a 5 by 5 and five 1s: six. Two 3 by 3 squares over three 2 by 2 squares make five. Four can’t: the only four square numbers that add to 30 are 16 + 9 + 4 + 1, and a 4 by 4 and a 3 by 3 can’t sit apart in 6 by 5 (4 + 3 is more than 6 across and more than 5 down). Three would be 25 + 4 + 1, where the 5 and the 2 clash the same way, and two square numbers never make 30.
parent.extension: Find another rectangle where biggest first is not fewest. (Puzzle 8.)
parent.connection: A greedy choice need not be the best one.

puzzles.provenance: Week 32 bonus Problems 1 and 2: the rule’s six against the fewest, five, on 6 by 5.

puzzles.instruction: Fill the rectangle with 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares, or press Can’t and pick rows or columns that each need their own 3 by 3 square, more than fit.

Can’t comes after a try, with at least one square on the board. Then pick rows, or columns, that each need a 3 by 3 square of their own, more of them than 3 by 3 squares fit. One 3 by 3 square crosses three neighbouring lines, so picked lines are at least three apart; a row and a column can share one.
puzzles.idea: Area 30 is two 9s and three 4s, and they fit: a strip of 3s over a strip of 2s.
puzzles.prerequisites: Telling odd lengths from even; counting to 7. Reading the Can’t rule with a grown-up the first time.
hints: A column of 5 can’t be all 2s.
Fill a 6 by 3 strip with 3 by 3 squares.
Two 3 by 3 squares on top, three 2 by 2 squares below.

parent.notice: Whether your child reuses the five-square filling from puzzle 4.
parent.prompt: Why does 6 by 5 fill when 5 by 5 does not?
parent.explanation: Two 3 by 3 squares fill a 6 by 3 strip and three 2 by 2 squares a 6 by 2 strip. A rectangle with both sides at least 2 fills with 2s and 3s exactly when both sides are even, or both are multiples of 3, or one side is a multiple of 6; here 6 is.
parent.connection: Which rectangles two square sizes fill is a classical tiling question; area alone does not decide it.

puzzles.provenance: Week 32 bonus Problem 3, the 6 by 5 board.

puzzles.title: Last square 3
puzzles.objective: Make three rectangles, up to 12 by 12, whose last square is 3, each with a different first square. Press Cut to run the biggest-square rule.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make three rectangles with last square 3 and different first squares.
puzzles.instruction: Make three rectangles, up to 12 by 12, whose last square is 3, each with a different first square. Press Cut to run the biggest-square rule.
puzzles.controls: Tap a square of the grid to stretch the rectangle to it, or drag its corner; arrow keys move the corner too. Press Cut to run the biggest-square rule, and change the rectangle to try again.
rules: Cut runs the rule. The biggest-square rule cuts the largest square from one end of the rectangle and repeats on what is left. The last square it cuts is ringed.
The first square is the first one cut.
A rectangle whose last square is 3 is kept, unless one with the same first square is kept already.
puzzles.idea: The last square measures both sides, so every side is a multiple of 3; first squares 6 and 9 need 9 by 6 and 12 by 9.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading numbers up to 15. The app runs the rule; multiplication facts help to plan.
hints: Try a few rectangles and cut each one. Which ones end on a 3?
Every side is a multiple of 3. Which rectangle starts with a 6 and still ends on a 3?
9 by 6 starts with a 6, and 12 by 9 with a 9.

parent.notice: Whether your child switches to sides that are multiples of 3 after a few cuts.
parent.prompt: Why must both sides be multiples of 3?
parent.explanation: The last square is the largest square whose equal copies fill the rectangle, so 3 divides both sides and no bigger number divides both. Within 12 the sides are 3, 6, 9 or 12, and the first square is the shorter side. First square 3: 3 by 3, 6 by 3, 9 by 3 or 12 by 3. First square 6 needs 9 as the other side (6 by 12 ends on 6), and first square 9 needs 12. So every answer has 9 by 6 and 12 by 9.
parent.extension: Make three rectangles within 12 that end on 2, with different first squares.
parent.connection: Euclid’s algorithm: the last square is the greatest common divisor.

puzzles.provenance: Week 32 grades 2–3 Problem 6: three rectangles with different first squares and last square 3, sides from 3, 6, 9 and 12.

puzzles.title: Five by five
puzzles.objective: Fill the rectangle with 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares, or press Can’t and pick rows or columns that each need their own 3 by 3 square, more than fit.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the rectangle with 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares, or press Can’t and pick rows or columns that each need their own 3 by 3 square, more than fit.
puzzles.controls: Drag from one corner of a square to the opposite corner, or tap the two corners; tap one square twice for the smallest square. Tap a square to lift it; Clear lifts them all. Only 2 by 2 and 3 by 3 squares. Once a square is down, Can’t puts a tab beside each row and below each column: tap tabs to pick lines, and tap a tab again to drop it.

Solved when the rectangle is full, or with a right Can’t.

Can’t comes after a try, with at least one square on the board. Then pick rows, or columns, that each need a 3 by 3 square of their own, more of them than 3 by 3 squares fit. One 3 by 3 square crosses three neighbouring lines, so picked lines are at least three apart; a row and a column can share one.
puzzles.idea: Rows 1 and 4 each need their own 3 by 3 square, and two never fit in 5 by 5.
puzzles.prerequisites: Telling odd lengths from even; counting to 7. Reading the Can’t rule with a grown-up the first time.
hints: Try to fill it. Where can a 3 by 3 square go?
Every row of 5 needs a 3 by 3 square across it. Can one cross both row 1 and row 4?
Press Can’t and tap rows 1 and 4.

parent.notice: Whether your child sees that area (25 is four 4s and a 9) is not enough.
parent.prompt: Why do rows 1 and 4 need different 3s?
parent.explanation: A row of 5 can’t be all 2s, so a 3 by 3 square crosses every row. One crosses three neighbouring rows, so rows 1 and 4 need two different ones. Two 3 by 3 squares never fit in 5 by 5: 3 + 3 is more than 5 across and down. The bonus guide argues the same way along the top and bottom edges.
parent.extension: Which squares fill with 2s and 3s? (Those with an even side or a side that is a multiple of 3.)
parent.connection: Packing bounds: a rectangle holds at most (width ÷ 3) × (height ÷ 3) squares of side 3, rounding down.

puzzles.provenance: Week 32 bonus Problem 3, the 5 by 5 board.

puzzles.title: Seven by six
puzzles.objective: Fill the rectangle with as few squares as you can, then press Done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with as few squares as you can.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the rectangle with as few squares as you can, then press Done.
puzzles.controls: Drag from one corner of a square to the opposite corner, or tap the two corners; tap one square twice for the smallest square. Tap a square to lift it; Clear lifts them all. Press Done when you think no filling uses fewer squares.
rules: Squares of any whole size, with edges on the grid lines, no gaps and no overlaps.
Done says no filling uses fewer squares. The app checks; if fewer fit, it says so, and that count stays answered.
puzzles.idea: The rule cuts a 6 and six 1s; five fit: a 4, two 3s and two 2s.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start: drag squares from corner to corner. Counting to about ten; square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25) help explain why fewer can’t fit.
hints: Count the biggest-square way first.
Try a 4 by 4 in a corner.
4 by 4 at the top left, two 3 by 3 squares down the right, two 2 by 2 squares under the 4.

parent.notice: Whether your child looks for squares whose sides add up to 7 and to 6.
parent.prompt: Which two squares fit across the top exactly?
parent.explanation: The rule uses a 6 by 6 and six 1s: seven. Five fit: a 4 by 4 in a corner, two 3 by 3 squares in the strip 3 wide beside it, two 2 by 2 squares under the 4. Four can’t: the only ways to make 42 from four square numbers are 36 + 4 + 1 + 1, 25 + 9 + 4 + 4 and 16 + 16 + 9 + 1, and each has two squares whose sides add to more than 7, which can’t sit apart; three would be 25 + 16 + 1, with the same clash.
parent.extension: Is there a rectangle where the rule uses twice as many as the fewest? (10 by 9: ten against six.)
parent.connection: Two squares that don’t overlap sit side by side or one above the other, so their sides fit across or down.

puzzles.provenance: New: another rectangle where the rule is not fewest, after Week 32 bonus Problems 1 and 2.

puzzles.title: Recipe 2, 1, 2
puzzles.objective: Make a rectangle, up to 12 by 12, that the biggest-square rule cuts into 2 equal squares, then 1 smaller square, then 2 smaller still. Press Cut to check.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make a rectangle whose cuts follow the card.
puzzles.instruction: Make a rectangle, up to 12 by 12, that the biggest-square rule cuts into 2 equal squares, then 1 smaller square, then 2 smaller still. Press Cut to check.
puzzles.controls: Tap a square of the grid to stretch the rectangle to it, or drag its corner; arrow keys move the corner too. Press Cut to run the biggest-square rule, and change the rectangle to try again.
rules: Cut runs the rule. The biggest-square rule cuts the largest square from one end of the rectangle and repeats on what is left. The last square it cuts is ringed.
The first square is the first one cut.
The card counts the squares of each size the rule cuts, largest size first: 2, then 1, then 2. The sizes are left out.
puzzles.idea: Build backwards from the smallest squares: two 1s make 2 by 1, one 2 makes 3 by 2, two 3s make 8 by 3.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading numbers up to 15. The app runs the rule; multiplication facts help to plan.
hints: Start from the end: the last two squares are equal and make a small rectangle together.
Two 1 by 1 squares make 2 by 1. One square on its long side makes the rectangle before it.
8 by 3: the rule cuts 3, 3, then 2, then 1, 1.

parent.notice: Whether your child builds from the last squares or tries sizes at random.
parent.prompt: Could a bigger rectangle follow the same card?
parent.explanation: Backwards: two equal last squares of side 1 make 2 by 1. One square on its long side makes 3 by 2. Two squares of 3 on that make 8 by 3. Doubling every length (16 by 6) keeps the card, so a card fixes a rectangle’s shape, not its size; within 12 by 12 only 8 by 3 (or 3 by 8) follows it. The card is the continued fraction 8/3 = 2 + 1/(1 + 1/2).
parent.extension: Find the rectangle for the card 1, 1, 3. (7 by 4.)
parent.connection: The counts are the partial quotients of the continued fraction of long side over short side.

puzzles.idea: Columns 1, 4 and 7 each need their own 3 by 3 square, and only two fit side by side.
puzzles.prerequisites: Telling odd lengths from even; counting to 7. Reading the Can’t rule with a grown-up the first time.
hints: Try to fill it. How many 3 by 3 squares fit at once?
Every column of 5 needs a 3 by 3 square across it. Which columns need different ones?
Press Can’t and tap columns 1, 4 and 7.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries rows first, and why rows of 7 don’t settle it.
parent.prompt: Why can’t three 3 by 3 squares fit?
parent.explanation: A column of 5 can’t be all 2s, so a 3 by 3 square crosses every column, and columns 1, 4 and 7 need three different ones. Two 3 by 3 squares in a rectangle 5 tall always share a row (3 + 3 is more than 5), so they sit side by side, and three need 9 across where there are 7. Area allows it (35 is two 4s and three 9s), which is why area alone does not decide.
parent.extension: Which widths fill when the rectangle is 5 tall? (Multiples of 6.)
parent.connection: The lines and the 3s that fit are a certificate: a short reason anyone can check.

puzzles.title: Thirteen by eleven
puzzles.objective: Fill the rectangle with as few squares as you can, then press Done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Fill it with as few squares as you can.
puzzles.instruction: Fill the rectangle with as few squares as you can, then press Done.
puzzles.controls: Drag from one corner of a square to the opposite corner, or tap the two corners; tap one square twice for the smallest square. Tap a square to lift it; Clear lifts them all. Press Done when you think no filling uses fewer squares.

hints: The rule uses eight. Try a different first square.
Try a 7 by 7 in one corner and a 6 by 6 beside it.
7 and 6 across the top; under them a 4, a 4, a 1 and a 5.

parent.notice: Whether your child gives up the biggest square and looks for sides that add to 13 and 11.
parent.prompt: Which two squares fit across the top exactly?
parent.explanation: The rule uses an 11, then five 2s and two 1s: eight. Six fit: 7 and 6 across the top, then 4, 4, a 1 and a 5 below. Showing that five can’t is a long case check; the app’s search tries every way.
parent.extension: What does the rule give for 13 by 8? (Six squares in five sizes: puzzle 12.)
parent.connection: How few squares can tile a rectangle is a research question (Kenyon, 1996).

puzzles.title: Five sizes
puzzles.objective: Make a rectangle, up to 15 by 15, that the biggest-square rule cuts into squares of five different sizes. Press Cut to check.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make a rectangle whose cuts have five different sizes.
puzzles.instruction: Make a rectangle, up to 15 by 15, that the biggest-square rule cuts into squares of five different sizes. Press Cut to check.
puzzles.controls: Tap a square of the grid to stretch the rectangle to it, or drag its corner; arrow keys move the corner too. Press Cut to run the biggest-square rule, and change the rectangle to try again.
rules: Cut runs the rule. The biggest-square rule cuts the largest square from one end of the rectangle and repeats on what is left. The last square it cuts is ringed.
The first square is the first one cut.
puzzles.idea: Each size is at least the next two together, so the sides grow like 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13: 13 by 8 is the only one within 15.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading numbers up to 15. The app runs the rule; multiplication facts help to plan.
hints: Small squares come last. Build up from the end: a 1, then a 2, then a 3.
Each size is at least the sum of the next two.

parent.notice: Whether your child builds up from small squares, or tries rectangles one after another.
parent.prompt: Why do the sides of the best rectangle go 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13?
parent.explanation: Each new size is one division step of Euclid’s algorithm. The sides shrink slowest when each step cuts one square, until the last cuts two; then each size is the sum of the next two, and the sides are Fibonacci numbers: 3 by 2, 5 by 3, 8 by 5 and 13 by 8 for five sizes. Within 15, 13 by 8 (turned or not) is the only rectangle with five; six need 21 by 13.
parent.extension: Which rectangles within 15 have four sizes? (Eight, up to turning: 8 by 5, 13 by 5, 11 by 7, 12 by 7, 11 by 8, 14 by 9, 14 by 11 and 15 by 11.)
parent.connection: Lamé (1844): Euclid’s algorithm takes the most steps on consecutive Fibonacci numbers.

puzzles.provenance: Week 32 grades 4–5 Problem 6 (the most different sizes, longer side 9 to 15 and shorter 2 to 8), set here as a target within 15 by 15.
